successors.name: Roman Republic
successors.text: Celtiberia: the Arevaci, Belli, Titti and Lusones

ledger.x: c. 500 BC: the Celtiberians' 'cultural stronghold in the northern central meseta, in the upper Tagus and Douro valleys east to the Ebro, in the modern provinces of Soria, Guadalajara, Zaragoza, and Teruel'; tribes Arevaci (Okilis), Belli and Titti (Jalon), Lusones, Pellendones; towns Numantia, Segeda, Termantia…
195 BC: 'part of Celtiberia was conquered in 195 BC' (Cato); uprising 195-193.
195-193 BC: 'Uprising, after part of Celtiberia was conquered in 195 BC'.
181-179 BC: the First Celtiberian War; Gracchus 'spent 182 to 179 BC pacifying the region and boasted of destroying over 300 settlements'.
154-151 BC: 'It began in 154 BC as a revolt of the Celtiberians of Numantia' (Segeda's revolt 154, Nobilior's defeat 153); 'the first phase of the war ended in 151'.
143-133 BC: 'in 143, war flared up again with a new insurrection in Numantia'; Mancinus' forced treaty (136) unratified; Scipio 'was sent in 134 BC and built a ring of seven fortresses'.
133 BC: Numantia falls, 'most of the surviving Numantines committed suicide rather than surrender to Rome'; the town razed; 'Expansion of the Roman territory through Celtiberia'.

133 BC: the end of Celtiberian independence; 'an era of lasting peace in Hispania until the Sertorian War', in which the cities' 'last formal resistance' (80-72) ended with 'the entire region' in Hispania Citerior by 72.

certainty.note: The eastern Meseta by modern provinces; the Vaccaei are 'only occasionally included' and are left out.

sources.title: Roman conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
